scenes.heading: CSV Format
scenes.subheading: The simplest way to exchange tabular data
scenes.narration: CSV, short for comma-separated values, is a plain-text format that stores tabular data as rows of values separated by commas.

scenes.heading: Why CSV is so common
scenes.narration: CSV is human-readable because it is just plain text you can open in any editor. It is supported almost everywhere, from spreadsheets to databases. It is simple to generate and parse, needing only a few lines of code. And it carries no dependencies, so it works without any special software.

scenes.heading: Parsing CSV in Python
scenes.code:
import csv

with open("customers.csv") as f:
    reader = csv.DictReader(f)
    for row in reader:
        print(row["name"], row["email"])
scenes.narration: This snippet reads a CSV file using Python's built-in csv module. DictReader treats the first line as a header, so each row becomes a dictionary keyed by column name. That lets us access fields by name like row of name and email. The simplicity of this code reflects why CSV remains so widely used for data exchange.

scenes.heading: CSV strengths and weaknesses
scenes.narration: CSV's strengths are that it is universal, readable, and trivial to produce. Its weaknesses are that it carries no data types or schema, offers no compression, and can be ambiguous when values contain commas or quotes. Those trade-offs are why analytical systems often prefer binary formats instead.

scenes.text: CSV is perfect for simple, portable data exchange but weak for large-scale analytics.
scenes.narration: In summary, reach for CSV when you need simple, portable exchange, but choose a richer format for large-scale analytical workloads.
